name: cat
one_line: concatenate files and print them on the standard output
plain: `cat` prints files, one after another. It is the simplest way to read a small file, join files together, or send a file into another command.
Its options also reveal invisible characters (tabs, line endings, control codes), which matters when a file looks right but behaves wrong.
when: Read a short file or a flag file.
See hidden characters such as tabs and Windows line endings (cat -A).

options.plain: Show everything: line ends as $, tabs as ^I and other control characters visibly (same as -vET).
options.use: Finding invisible characters in a file.

options.plain: Number the non-empty lines only. This overrides -n.
Same as -vE: show line ends and control characters.
options.use: Spotting trailing spaces and Windows line endings.

options.plain: Print a $ at the end of every line.
Collapse several blank lines into one.
Same as -vT: show tabs as ^I and control characters visibly.
Ignored; kept so that old scripts still work.
options.use: You will almost never need it.

options.plain: Show control characters with ^ and M- notation (everything except line feed and tab).
options.use: Seeing escape codes and binary junk.

options.plain: Print a short usage message and exit.

mistakes: Using cat file | grep when grep file works (it is harmless, but slower and longer).
Running cat on a binary file: the terminal can fill with strange characters; use cat -v or strings instead (reset fixes a garbled terminal).
cat file > file empties the file before reading it.
try: Find trailing spaces in a file with cat -E.
Check whether a file has Windows line endings with cat -A.
Join three files into one and number the lines.
Make a garbled terminal with cat on a binary file, then repair it with reset.
see_also: less(1), head(1), tail(1), tac(1) (reverse), nl(1), od(1), xxd(1), bat for a nicer viewer.
